prompt: Match each number to who sets it.

pairs.left: The weights of a logistic regression
The break-even chance for sending a credit

prompt: Why can't `fit` choose a hyperparameter the way it chooses a weight?
hint: Each value gives a different model.

choices.text: They do not affect the model's quality
choices.why: The grid's worst and best differ by R$ 500 per thousand rows.

choices.text: scikit-learn forbids it by design, for reasons of speed on large tables
choices.why: It is not a rule of the library; it is how the problem is shaped.

choices.text: Hyperparameters are always integers
choices.why: The learning rate is not.

choices.text: Its quality is only known after fitting a model with it
choices.why: Yes. So values are tried and scored on validation data.

prompt: Why does `tuning.py` score each candidate on time folds rather than random ones?
hint: What would a search on flattering folds pick?

choices.text: Flattering folds reward flattery
choices.why: Yes. The folds must look like the situation the model will be in.

choices.text: Time folds are faster
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: Random folds would include the test months
choices.why: `by_time` removes them before any folds are made.

choices.text: Grid search refuses random folds
choices.why: It accepts any folds.

prompt: What would go wrong if the search used scikit-learn's default score for a classifier?

choices.text: It would tune the threshold instead of the model, and send credits to everybody in the end
choices.why: Accuracy uses 0.5 and tunes nothing about the threshold.

choices.text: It would pick by accuracy, a number that barely moves on this data while the money moves a lot
choices.why: Yes. Accuracy hides the money, as lesson 2 showed.

choices.text: It would refuse to run
choices.why: It runs; it optimises the wrong thing.

choices.text: It would leak the test months
choices.why: The score does not decide which rows are used.

prompt: What did the defaults score, on average, in `baseline_cv.py`, in reais per thousand rows?
A grid tries 4 learning rates, 3 tree sizes and 5 numbers of trees, with 3 folds. How many fits is that?
The grid's top five differ by 52 reais per thousand rows, and each has a standard deviation of 132 to 193 across folds. What is the honest summary?
hint: Compare the gap with the spread.

choices.text: Tuning makes no difference
choices.why: Best and worst differ by R$ 500.

choices.text: The grid was too small and must be redone with ten values of each of the three dials
choices.why: A larger grid would multiply the cost and the luck.

choices.text: Small trees are better here
choices.why: Yes. That pattern is real; the exact order is mostly luck.

choices.text: The first row is the best setting
choices.why: The gap is far smaller than the spread.

prompt: Why does random search usually beat a grid of the same size?
hint: Look at the tick marks in the figure.

choices.text: It fits fewer models
choices.why: Same budget, 18 candidates each.

choices.text: It uses the test months
choices.why: It uses the same folds as the grid.

choices.text: Random numbers are luckier
choices.why: It is geometry, not luck.

choices.text: More values of each dial
choices.why: Yes. No two random points share a coordinate.

prompt: Why is the learning rate drawn with `loguniform(0.01, 0.5)` rather than evenly between the two?
hint: Is going from 0.01 to 0.02 a small change?

choices.text: Its effect is proportional
choices.why: Yes. Evenly, almost every draw would land above 0.05.

choices.text: Small learning rates are always best
choices.why: The best found was about 0.1.

choices.text: To make the search finish faster
choices.why: The distribution does not change how many fits are made.

choices.text: scikit-learn rejects uniform distributions
choices.why: It accepts them; `randint` is one.

prompt: What was random search's best score, in reais per thousand rows?
What does Bayesian search do that grid and random search do not?
hint: It looks at the results so far.

choices.text: It never explores regions it has not tried
choices.why: It does, when their uncertainty is large.

choices.text: It chooses each next setting from a model of the scores so far
choices.why: Yes. A Gaussian process here, with expected improvement.

choices.text: It tries every combination
choices.why: That is a grid.

choices.text: It needs no validation data
choices.why: Every point is still scored on the folds.

prompt: The rule that picks the next point, counting both a high guess and a wide uncertainty, is expected ___.
hint: How much it beats the best so far.

prompt: Tries 13, 15 and 18 of `bayes_search.py` score much lower than the tries around them. Is that waste?
hint: What would a search that only refined do?

choices.text: Yes, those points should have been skipped
choices.why: Nobody knew they were poor before trying them.

choices.text: Yes, the search lost its way
choices.why: It went back to the good region right after.

choices.text: No: exploration
choices.why: Yes. Without exploring, it settles on the first good region.

choices.text: No; low scores are the best ones
choices.why: Higher is better for this scorer.

prompt: Why are a search's best validation scores optimistic?

choices.text: Validation folds are smaller than the test
choices.why: Size is not the cause.

choices.text: Validation data is always easier than test data, because it comes from earlier months
choices.why: Not always; the bias comes from choosing.

choices.text: Cross-validation double-counts each row
choices.why: Each row is scored once.

choices.text: The winner is partly the luckiest
choices.why: Yes. The more tried, the more the best owes to luck.

prompt: Tuned R$ 22,464, defaults R$ 21,248 on the test months. How much more did tuning make, in reais?
The interval for *tuned minus defaults* runs from −R$ 1,001 to R$ 3,457. What should Ana report?

choices.text: A better bet by about a thousand reais, with wide uncertainty
choices.why: Yes. And no further tuning on the same months.

choices.text: Run a new search until the interval stops crossing zero
choices.why: That chases luck and, done on the test, ruins it.

choices.text: Tuning was useless and should be reverted
choices.why: It is still the better bet.

choices.text: Tuning added R$ 1,216, proven
choices.why: The interval crosses zero; it is not proven.

prompt: Put a sensible tuning plan in order.
hint: Coarse before fine, the test last.
items: Fix the folds and the score
Random search over wide log ranges
A narrower search around the best region
Score the chosen setting once on the test

prompt: Which of these make a tuning budget go further? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Checking the test after each search to steer the next
choices.why: That turns the test into validation.

choices.text: Stopping when gains fall inside the noise
choices.why: Yes. Past that, features pay more.

choices.text: Searching the dials that matter most
choices.why: Yes. Dials that change nothing waste fits.

choices.text: Letting early stopping set the number of trees
choices.why: Yes. It removes the costliest dial.
